Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Vignette:
When Tano’s son was six, a sudden respiratory distress turned an ordinary Tuesday into a prolonged ordeal inside the emergency wing. Tano had come to believe that the moment the child’s oxygen mask slipped and the monitors began their sharp, rhythmic alarms, the timeline fractured. He was certain that the antiseptic smell clinging to his jacket that afternoon would haunt him for years. Even now, at seventy-five, when he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread and cannot finish, his words tangling around the sharp edges of the event. His memories of the frightening episode play like a film over and over, each time cutting to the exact second the physician leaned over the gurney. He feels the past as present; the sterile corridor does not fade into a distant memory but occupies the same physical space as the here and now. His daily routine as a cybersecurity analyst now folds these triggers into the quiet hum of his home office. He spends his days monitoring network traffic on expansive screens, a role that keeps him alert to subtle shifts in pattern. During a routine annual physical last month, the clinic’s aggressive hospital smell hit him while he was sitting on the examination table. He had to pause the nurse’s questions, certain the room was tilting back toward that emergency wing. The medical procedure itself—a stethoscope pressed against his chest and an IV line inserted—became a concrete anchor for his discomfort. He was not merely undergoing a checkup; he was enduring the same clinical scrutiny that had once surrounded his child. Weeks later, when he took the bus past a new maternity ward, the sight of parents carrying newborns in swaddling blankets triggered a sudden, unbidden wave of negative emotions. He had come to believe that life, in its fragile beginning, carried the same weight it had held in the hospital beds. Over the years, these responses have accumulated into a steady pattern. When a trigger strikes, Tano experiences strong physical reactivity; his pulse quickens and his shoulders tighten as if bracing for an alarm. Fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame surface without warning. Flashbacks arrive as vivid intrusions, making him feel as though the stressful experience is actually happening again. He avoids discussing the illness directly, navigating around pregnancy and birth reminders by choosing alternative routes home. His avoidance developed over weeks and months into a quiet habit; he stopped attending neighborhood family gatherings where babies were present, citing busy work schedules, while his personal world narrowed to spare him sudden sensory shifts. His cybersecurity work remained unaffected; he still reads threat alerts and logs hours, but his daily environment reflects this deliberate pacing. A PCL-5 score of seventy-four maps cleanly onto this substantial, co-existing burden. What finally brought Tano to seek help was not a single dramatic event, but the steady accumulation of these moments. He noticed how the olfactory reminder from a recent clinic visit, the medical procedures during routine care, and the sight of newborns along his commute had begun to occupy his days with equal weight. What frightened him most was the possibility that the film-like memories would continue to press against his present. He is seeking a way to sit in a room, to hear a trigger without his mind jumping backward, and to explain what happened without losing the thread. At seventy-five, widowed after decades of shared years, Tano sits at his desk, the screens reflecting the same careful attention they always have, ready to face the years ahead with a clearer, steadier gaze.
